docs.title: Scalability
docs.text:
CSG reconstruction time scales with the number of IN cells (geometric complexity) rather than the total number of faces. The PMC sampling approach discovers only geometrically reachable sign vectors, making the theoretical 2^n cell count irrelevant in practice.

Faces Theoretical 2^n Actual IN Cells CSG Time 6 64 5 0.5s 139 10^41 185 2.7s 270 10^81 1,375 6.5s 518 10^155 4,901 18.0s 664 10^199 4,108 63.8s

The relationship is approximately linear in the number of IN cells, with an additional factor for sampling convergence.

docs.title: BSpline Performance
docs.text:
A fast sign determination method (bounding box pruning + surface center normal dot product) eliminates the Newton projection bottleneck during PMC sampling. BSpline faces add negligible overhead when they occupy a small fraction of the part.

Comparison Faces BSpline Time FTC-08 (no BSpline) 270 0 6.5s FTC-07 (20 BSpline) 269 20 6.6s

docs.title: Known Limitations
docs.text:
1. Large BSpline-heavy parts: OCCT linkrods (49% BSpline) takes 58s. Bounding box pruning is less effective when BSpline faces cover most of the part.

  2. Resolution vs accuracy: Grid-based volume at resolution 32 gives 0.3% error for NURBS shapes (vs 0.036% for analytical primitives).

  3. Thin features: Very thin walls or narrow slots may be missed by random sampling if the feature volume is small relative to the bounding box. Increasing samples_per_round mitigates this.

docs.title: Comparison with Feasibility Predictions
docs.text: Prediction Actual "20 faces is practical limit" 664 faces successful "BSpline SDF is high risk" 100% conversion, fast sign for PMC "97-98% analytical faces" 97.5% analytical (confirmed) "Rational B-spline needs weights" 56 rational faces converted with weights

docs.title: NURBS Differentiation Scope
docs.text: Differentiating a parametric surface, a trimmed face, and a closed CAD solid are distinct problems. BRepAX implements parts of each, but their derivative contracts cannot be interchanged. The API overview records supported inputs and numerical assumptions.

docs.title: Surface evaluation and distance
docs.text:
A rational B-spline surface maps parameters (u, v) to a point using control points, knot vectors, degrees, and weights. JAX evaluation exposes derivatives of this map with the array shapes and degrees fixed.

BSplineSurface.sdf adds a closest-point problem. It chooses an initial parameter pair from coarse samples and runs Newton projection on squared distance. The sign comes from surface normals, using precomputed coarse normals when available. An open patch does not by itself define the inside of a closed solid.

The implemented derivative follows the unrolled Newton iterations in brepax.nurbs.projection, with the discrete initial-sample choice held fixed. It is not an implicit derivative of an exactly converged global minimum. Multiple closest points, clipping at parameter bounds, or a change in the selected initial sample can affect differentiability. Projection convergence and independent distance/gradient checks therefore matter in addition to surface-evaluation accuracy.

The earlier prototype proposal on this page recommended implicit differentiation before the current implementation existed. That remains a possible alternative, not the implemented contract or an approved solver migration.

docs.title: Trimming and solid composition
docs.text:
A trim polygon restricts a face in parameter space. A nearest point on the underlying surface can lie outside that polygon; the distance to a trimmed face then also depends on its boundary. BRepAX has trim metadata and standalone face-distance wrappers for this purpose.

Combining those face distances into a solid is a separate operation. A finite-face distance does not necessarily carry the half-space sign needed by a CSG intersection. The attempt to substitute a Marschner trim-aware blend inside the CSG-Stump DNF was rejected for analytical surfaces and B-splines. ADR-0020 records the counterexample and current use of raw primitive SDFs. Retaining trim metadata alone does not make that composition trim-aware or resolve its phantom-volume failure cases.

docs.title: Solid metrics and geometry edits
docs.text:
The mesh path uses OCCT tessellation followed by JAX surface evaluation and mesh integrals. It avoids using an approximate solid SDF for volume, but its derivatives depend on which data are allowed to move:

  • With fixed connectivity and UV samples, AD differentiates the chosen mesh evaluation. CAD reconstruction and tessellation are outside that graph.
  • Moving a surface without moving its neighboring trim boundaries can open the mesh. Shared boundary motion must be part of the parameterization.
  • Rebuilt CAD and fresh meshing supply a separate reference for an edit. Agreement on one fixed discretization does not establish agreement after reconstruction or through a change in topology.

The CAD editing benchmark provides a bounded roof/through-hole family with coupled boundary motion. Its JAX/AD evaluations use a shared working mesh. Finite-difference reference derivatives rebuild CAD at each perturbed dimension. The inverse-edit benchmark separately checks rebuilt CAD, fresh meshing, and STEP roundtrips after rigid transformations and unit changes. These checks apply to the supplied family; they do not establish arbitrary STEP editing, derivatives through remeshing, or topology-changing edits.

docs.title: Evidence needed for broader claims
docs.text:
For a new surface or edit family, check values against an independent geometric reference and derivatives against analytic results or a finite-difference step sweep. Include non-convex projection cases, trim boundaries, closure, orientation, units, and near-degenerate inputs when they are relevant to the claimed capability.

Rigid transformations and changes of units should be assessed for both values and gradients. Transform external directions with the geometry and scale dimensional tolerances consistently. Separate discretization error from violations of the geometric law, and distinguish a transformed fixed mesh from transformed CAD followed by fresh meshing.

Neither primitive-level stratum tests nor fixed-topology mesh derivatives establish a general differentiable NURBS Boolean kernel. That broader claim needs independent evidence across changing intersections and trim topology.

docs.title: Stratification Theory
docs.text: Boolean relations help organize geometric derivatives, but a topology change does not by itself imply a first-derivative jump. The objective, local contact geometry, and numerical discretization must be specified.

docs.title: Relation Regions and Contact Sets
docs.text:
For disks or spheres with positive radii and center distance \(d\):

Label Relationship Strict region 0 Disjoint \(d > r_1+r_2\) 1 Partial overlap \(\lvert r_1-r_2\rvert < d < r_1+r_2\) 2 A strictly contained in B \(d+r_1 < r_2\) 3 B strictly contained in A \(d+r_2 < r_1\)

These operational labels are not a complete Whitney stratification. External tangency, internal tangency, and equal-radius coincidence require separate sets. All four strict regions are full-dimensional; partial overlap is not uniquely highest-dimensional. A Whitney stratification additionally requires smooth strata, frontier conditions, and Whitney regularity, none of which follows from four labels.

For union measure, disjoint and contained formulas reduce to \(V_A+V_B\), \(V_B\), and \(V_A\), respectively. Partial overlap requires intersection measure. Exact primitive-volume derivatives therefore help without solving the harder contact problem.

docs.title: Contact Order for Area and Volume
docs.text:
Let \(\delta>0\) denote normal penetration from first contact. For a smooth \(m\)-dimensional contact set in \(n\) dimensions, suppose the local gap in the \(k=n-1-m\) transverse tangent directions is, to leading order,

\[ \delta-\tfrac12 y^\top H y,\qquad H\text{ positive definite}. \]

Integrating its positive part gives changed measure proportional to \(\delta^{1+k/2}\). This local model assumes nondegenerate relative curvature, a regular contact set, and no simultaneous endpoint event.

Geometry and objective Leading change as \(\delta\downarrow0\) Contact regularity Two disks, overlap area \(C\delta^{3/2}\) First derivative continuous; second derivative unbounded Two spheres, overlap volume \(C\delta^2\) First derivative continuous; second derivative jumps Parallel finite cylinders, side contact with positive common axial length \(C\delta^{3/2}\) First derivative continuous Opposing planar faces with positive contact area \(A\) \(A\delta\) One-sided volume derivatives differ

Here \(C>0\) depends on geometry. Zero relative curvature, corners, contact endpoints, and coincident surfaces need separate analysis; contact dimension alone is not a universal classification.

For internal tangency with fixed radii \(R>r>0\), let \(\delta=d-(R-r)\). The excess union measure beyond the larger primitive satisfies

\[ A_{\mathrm{union}}-\pi R^2 \sim \frac43\sqrt{\frac{2Rr}{R-r}}\,\delta^{3/2}, \qquad V_{\mathrm{union}}-\frac{4\pi R^3}{3} \sim \frac{\pi Rr}{R-r}\,\delta^2. \]

Ordinary internal and external contacts are therefore both \(C^1\) for these area/volume objectives. The earlier assertion of a first-order jump at unequal-radius internal tangency was incorrect. Equal-radius coincidence is a distinct degeneracy not covered by this conclusion.

The objective also matters. For two unit spheres with \(d=2-\delta\), overlap volume is \(\pi\delta^2/2-\pi\delta^3/12\), whereas union surface area is \(8\pi-2\pi\delta\) for \(0<\delta<2\). Volume is \(C^1\) at first contact; surface area has a first-derivative kink. The overlap volume tends to zero continuously at first contact.

docs.title: Directional Response at Opposing Planar Contact
docs.text:
Let finite solids have disjoint interiors and meet on one isolated convex planar polygon \(M\), with positive thickness on both sides. Let \(n\) point out of the fixed solid toward the moving solid. For a rigid path with velocity \(w(x)=v+\omega\times(x-p)\) and dimensionless parameter \(t\), the positive one-sided intersection-volume response is

\[ D^+ V_{\cap}(v,\omega) =\lim_{t\downarrow0}\frac{V_{\cap}(t)-V_{\cap}(0)}{t} =\int_M [-n\cdot w(x)]_+\,dA. \]

Locally, normal displacement creates an overlap layer with thickness \(t[-n\cdot w(x)]_++O(t^2)\). The moving polygon edges affect strips of area \(O(t)\) and thickness \(O(t)\), so their volume does not contribute at first order. This bounded argument requires regular finite edges, fixed positive thickness, bounded velocities, and no other first-order boundary contribution.

For \(M=[-1,1]^2\) in the XY plane with pivot at the origin, the integrand is \([-v_z+\omega_y x-\omega_x y]_+\). Normal approach with \(v_z=-1\) gives 4; separation gives 0. Both unit tilts \(\omega_x=1\) and \(\omega_x=-1\) give 1. Consequently the response is positively homogeneous and subadditive, but not linear or odd. It cannot be represented by one ordinary gradient/JVP. The signed left derivative along a direction is \(-D^+V_{\cap}(-v,-\omega)\). Rigid union and stock-minus-tool volume responses have the opposite sign.

The experimental planar evaluator implements this direction-dependent integral. Its host CAD preparation returns a nominal projected support-polygon model with diagnostics. A positive source gap, existing volume overlap, an omitted positive-area contact, or co-oriented coincidence needs different geometric information; none is certified by a small OCCT residual. See the application contract and ADR-0022.

One-sided interior/exterior traces in Berggren (2023) explain the relevant approach/separation distinction. Its nonnegative basis perturbations do not directly state the mixed-sign rigid-tilt formula above, which follows from the local overlap argument. The cut-geometry AD results of Wegert et al. (2025) and Wegert et al. (2026) assume stable cut topology; in particular, the latter's Assumption 3.5 excludes birth of a full-dimensional overlap from this face contact. These are prior techniques, not a direct proof of this event or evidence of theoretical novelty here.

docs.title: Several simultaneous polyhedral contacts
docs.text:
Let each body be a finite union of full-dimensional convex polyhedral cells, with disjoint cell interiors within each body. All moving cells follow the same rigid path, and the two bodies initially have disjoint interiors. Then the component-pair intersections partition the total intersection up to measure-zero boundaries, even at finite displacement:

\[ |A\cap g_t(B)|=\sum_{i,j}|A_i\cap g_t(B_j)|. \]

Consequently, the positive one-sided volume response is the sum of the planar integrals over all positive-area component-pair contacts. Shared patch edges require no first-order correction. Duplicate or overlapping same-body cells invalidate this partition; their contributions cannot simply be added. Two initially disjoint convex bodies have a separating plane, so nonparallel contact patches require a nonconvex body or a union of cells.

Positive-gap pairs contribute zero for sufficiently small motion. Edge-only contacts contribute at most \(O(t^2)\) and vertex-only contacts at most \(O(t^3)\) for a fixed nondegenerate polyhedral configuration. They must still be kept in the geometry inventory: zero first-order response is not finite-motion safety. For example, diagonal motion into an edge can create volume \(t^2\). A cube moving into an L-shaped corner can instead give \(2t-t^2\): the two unit-area contacts contribute a first derivative of 2, while the finite difference quotient has an \(O(t)\) error. Bounds are not uniform as feature thicknesses or angles degenerate.

The summed response remains convex and positively homogeneous in the supplied rigid direction. It vanishes exactly when the separating normal velocity is nonnegative at every vertex of every convex contact polygon. These linear inequalities describe a cone of motions without first-order penetration, not a certificate for a finite edit. Cell ordering and nonoverlapping patch subdivision preserve the response, in addition to its rigid-motion, unit, and compensated-pivot laws.

This is a local polyhedral derivation using the measure partition above. Kiderlen and Rataj, Theorem 1.1 establishes a related positive-part boundary integral for dilation by finite translation sets. Schymura, Corollary 4 bounds changes of overlap under rigid motions; paths differing by \(O(t^2)\) therefore have the same first-order response in this bounded setting. Neither result is being cited as a theorem about arbitrary source CAD or as a novelty claim for this implementation.

docs.title: Finite translation and event intervals
docs.text:
For a prescribed translation \(B_t=B+t v\), each component-pair intersection has fixed plane normals and affine offsets:

\[ P(t)=\{x:n_k\cdot x\le b_k+t c_k\}. \]

An independent triple of planes defines a candidate vertex \(x(t)=a+t d\). Its remaining inequalities give an exact feasibility interval. Between these interval endpoints the active vertices and faces are fixed; a consistently oriented facet triangulation expresses volume as a sum of determinants of three affine vectors. Each determinant has degree at most three. Summing over the disjoint-interior cell pairs preserves this piecewise-polynomial structure. This is established parametric-polytope volume computation; see Verdoolaege, Section 5.9. It is not a new general Boolean differentiation theorem.

The experimental preparation derives these intervals and coefficients from the represented vertex hulls with rational arithmetic, without fitting sampled CAD volumes. The JAX evaluator uses floating coefficients and must retain their rounding limits. Geometry and translation direction are fixed by host preparation; differentiation with respect to step inside an open interval differentiates its polynomial. At an event, use the specified one-sided slope instead of assuming a unique derivative. The model is continuous in volume, but its derivatives need not be continuous.

For appropriately translating unit boxes, the first branches are \(t\), \(t^2\), and \(t^3\) for face, edge, and point contact. A positive gap postpones overlap until its entry event. Later exit events can make volume decrease, so neither zero initial response nor a missing sampled bracket establishes that finite overlap or a target is impossible. Finite models still require an independent CAD check when applied to source solids.

docs.title: Target positions along a finite path
docs.text:
For a target volume \(q\), solve \(V(t)-q=0\) on every prepared interval. A finite-body intersection can enter and leave the stock, attain the target several times, or have a constant-volume interval. Consequently a sign change between sampled endpoints is sufficient to locate some roots, but its absence does not establish that no root exists. A target at a local extremum can be a repeated root without a sign change.

The exact represented polynomial and target permit rational root counting and isolation, including repeated roots. Keep an isolating interval separate from a floating candidate that meets the requested step and volume tolerances. Failure to resolve such a candidate is a numerical outcome, not a proof of unreachability. Constant solution intervals are distinct from isolated roots. Range estimates likewise require the interval endpoints and interior stationary points, not just sampled values. Any reachability conclusion concerns only the represented geometry and supplied translation interval.

Polynomial inversion of geometric volume is established. For example, Kromer and Bothe, Section 2.4.1 use the cubic volume within a bracket to position a cutting plane without further geometric truncation there. Their plane-cut volume is monotone; that uniqueness assumption does not extend to a bounded cutter entering and leaving a solid.

docs.title: Design parameters and moving event boundaries
docs.text:
With fixed plane normals and affine dimension controls \(\theta\), consider

\[ P(t,\theta)=\{x:n_k\cdot x\le b_k+t c_k+d_k^\top\theta\}. \]

Independent plane triples give vertices affine in both \(t\) and \(\theta\). A remaining inequality has the form \(a+\beta t+\gamma^\top\theta\le0\). When \(\beta\ne0\), its candidate event is

\[ \tau(\theta)=-\frac{a+\gamma^\top\theta}{\beta},\qquad \partial_\theta\tau=-\frac{\gamma^\top}{\beta}. \]

A fixed ordering of these events and fixed active faces define a local parameter region. Within its event intervals, oriented facet determinants give volume polynomials of total degree at most three in \((t,\theta)\). Differentiating those polynomials includes the motion of the intersection vertices. This uses the same parametric-polytope principle as the fixed-path construction; it is not a new general shape-differentiation theorem. Wegert et al., Section 3.2 similarly propagate derivatives through cut vertices and maps while assuming stable cut topology under small perturbations.

The parameter region must also preserve valid, bounded, positive-volume cells, their fixed facet normals, and the disjoint-interior conditions used to sum component volumes. Checking these properties only at the reference parameter does not justify evaluation at another parameter. Conservative validity conditions need not describe the largest admissible region. Floating checks near a moving event require their own uncertainty policy; an exact host model does not make a rounded event comparison exact.

For numerical evaluation, expanding near a moving event reduces cancellation in the value. Differentiating that rounded normalization introduces another chain-rule cancellation, which can obscure a structurally zero design derivative. The parameter evaluator therefore uses a custom first-order JVP from the physical derivative polynomials collected before floating packing. It represents the same volume model and is linear in the step/design tangents; the host-prepared coefficients are not differentiation variables. Independent derivative references are necessary to validate this choice. A query whose value or intended derivative cannot be resolved numerically returns NaN, even when its exact host model is valid. Some smooth stationary configurations are consequently outside the numerical chart's accepted queries.

An event can be a redundant change of representation rather than physical contact. Moreover, events with distinct sensitivities can coincide: the first of \(1+\theta\) and \(1-\theta\) is \(1-|\theta|\). The strict parameter chart rejects that changing event order; its rejection does not prove that the underlying volume lacks a derivative. Zero crossing speed, event-order changes, and simultaneous events require separate treatment.

For a locally isolated target position \(t_*(\theta)\) inside an event interval, where \(V(t_*(\theta),\theta)=q(\theta)\) and \(\partial_t V\ne0\), the implicit function theorem gives

\[ \partial_\theta t_*= \frac{\partial_\theta q-\partial_\theta V}{\partial_t V}. \]

For a fixed physical target, its derivative is zero. If the target depends on \(\theta\), include its derivative. This local formula does not select between multiple roots, certify that an arbitrary query is a target root, or extend through a zero slope or event boundary. Event-time sensitivity is not an additive correction to a static Boolean volume derivative; see the TOI distinction.

docs.title: A supplied event-order exchange
docs.text:
For one design parameter, suppose exactly two distinct affine events \(\tau_1(\theta)\) and \(\tau_2(\theta)\) meet at an interior step \(t_0\) when \(\theta=0\). This is a codimension-one boundary in design space. Their lines intersect at a codimension-two point in the joint \((t,\theta)\) plane. Stable labels preserve each affine derivative; sorting the events can introduce a cusp, as in \(\min(1+\theta,1-\theta)=1-|\theta|\).

The bounded host construction prepares the two adjacent parameter regions, retains non-event validity conditions at zero, and checks that their polynomial closures agree with the exact fixed-parameter profile. It then selects incident pieces by the signs of an infinitesimal ray and evaluates

\[ D^+V(t_0,0;d_t,d_\theta)= \lim_{\epsilon\downarrow0} \frac{V(t_0+\epsilon d_t,\epsilon d_\theta)-V(t_0,0)}{\epsilon}. \]

This map is positively homogeneous but need not be linear. For two independent contacts with areas 1 and 2, unit normal speed, and onset times \(1+\theta\) and \(1-\theta\), respectively, the local response is \((d_t-d_\theta)_+ + 2(d_t+d_\theta)_+\), where \(x_+=\max(x,0)\). It cannot define a JVP. At fixed step, the signed left derivative is \(-D^+V(t_0,0;0,-1)\) and the right derivative is \(D^+V(t_0,0;0,1)\); here they are -1 and 2. Equality would establish an ordinary scalar parameter derivative, not a joint gradient. Tangent rays require agreement of all incident limits.

Event regularity, volume regularity and target-set regularity are different questions. The independent-contact example has a smooth small positive-target root through the exchange. A cutter attaining full coverage can instead change from no target solution to one position to a whole interval. The existing implicit inverse formula does not extend to those branch changes. This bounded construction uses the chamber-volume background above; it is not a general stratification, boundary search or TOI correction.

docs.title: Searching for a feasible design across the exchange
docs.text:
Let \(I\) be a compact closed parameter interval inside the boundary certificate, \(t\in[0,T]\), and \(V(t,\theta)\) the continuous overlap volume. The preparation contract gives \(V(0,\theta)=0\). For a positive lower target-band limit \(q_-\), therefore, a design is feasible precisely when

\[ M(\theta)=\max_{0\leq t\leq T} V(t,\theta)\ \geq\ q_-. \]

This follows from continuity in \(t\), not monotonicity. It does not imply that \(M\) is monotone or differentiable in \(\theta\), or that its feasible set is one interval. For example, a width/height tradeoff can leave both ends of \(I\) infeasible while an interior interval is feasible. At a limiting target that interval can shrink to an isolated point.

Split \(I\) at the supplied exchange. In each remaining interval \(J=[a,b]\), map each affine event strip to a unit square using its two affine step boundaries. The volume polynomial has degree at most three in each coordinate. Its tensor Bernstein coefficients enclose every value on that square, including collapsed strip boundaries. Let their largest upper bound be \(B_J\). This uses established polynomial range bounds, not a new differentiation rule.

Subdividing only \(\theta\) need not make \(B_J\) tight: the unsplit translation coordinate can retain overestimation. Instead, also bound the physical \(|\partial_\theta V|\) by \(L_J\) over every strip. At fixed \(t\), the finite piecewise-polynomial path is continuous through strip boundaries. Integrating these bounded derivatives and then maximizing over the same \([0,T]\) gives

\[ \sup_{\theta\in J} M(\theta) \leq \min\{B_J,\ \overline{M}(c)+L_J\max(c-a,b-c)\}, \qquad c=(a+b)/2, \]

where \(\overline{M}(c)\) is a conservative fixed-parameter maximum enclosure. The derivative must include the chain rule for the moving step normalization; it is not the derivative at a fixed normalized strip coordinate.

Discard \(J\) only when this upper bound is strictly below \(q_-\). The minimum of the distances from the initial parameter to all remaining intervals and the incumbent cost, when present, gives a global objective lower bound. A verified numerical edit supplies an upper bound. Their difference bounds how much a better feasible edit could improve the returned design. The witness is checked at its actual binary64 parameter and step using exact represented polynomials. An exact rational solution alone does not establish a usable float edit or source-CAD correctness.

Finite refinement, the fixed-range enclosure tolerance, and isolated solutions can leave the result unresolved. In particular, equality in a bound is not an infeasibility proof. The capped search terminates, but need not resolve feasibility or optimality. No global smoothness or gradient of the selected design is claimed. See the experimental query contract.

docs.title: Discovering adjacent parameter regions
docs.text:
In one parameter, each strict affine guard has at most one isolated rational root. The closest roots bound the current certified open interval. A root can mark the expiry of a sufficient cell, separation, or feasibility certificate; it need not change the physical overlap. This is the distinction between internal certificate events and output changes in kinetic data structures.

The bounded continuation handles a root only when every vanishing guard names the same isolated pair of interior translation events. It constructs the adjacent region with exact rational centers, checks event inventories and all guard closures, and compares both limiting polynomials with a separate exact fixed-parameter construction. The original affine family is preserved; rounded vertices at a new center would define a different family. Exact event ordering and independent static reconstruction are established techniques; see Russel, Karavelas, and Guibas, sections 4.4 and 5. These checks do not establish that every physically valid region can be reached.

Let \(H\) be the uncovered part of the requested closed design window, including any unconfirmed singleton endpoints. Every component \(J\) contributes \(\inf_{\theta\in J}|\theta-\theta_0|\) to the global objective lower bound, together with the bounds from unfinished searches and the incumbent cost. The width of an unknown interval is irrelevant to this rule: an arbitrarily small interval containing \(\theta_0\) has lower bound zero. A positive volume allowance can also leave an isolated feasible design at a local maximum. Conversely, a sufficiently distant unknown region need not prevent a valid objective-gap certificate. Whole-window infeasibility requires full coverage and exclusion of every covered region and point.

Physical values obey the same exact frame and unit laws on jointly certified inputs. The current choice of sufficient separating certificate can produce different coverage after a coordinate rotation, so coverage and resource-limited search status are not claimed to be equivariant. Equal-cost designs can also have different selected numerical witnesses. No ordinary gradient of boundary discovery or design selection follows from these host computations.

docs.title: Rotation depends on the full path
docs.text:
The finite benchmark uses \(x(t)=p+R(t\omega)(x-p)+t v\). Let \(\Omega x= \omega\mathbin{\times}x\). Replacing \(p\) by \(p+d\) and \(v\) by \(v+\Omega d\) preserves the initial velocity field, but changes the finite trajectory by

\[ (I-R(t\omega))d+t\Omega d=-\tfrac12t^2\Omega^2d+O(t^3). \]

This is a different physical path, not a violation of coordinate covariance. Consequently the earlier compensated-pivot law is a first-order law only.

For a prism \([0,w]\times[-a,b]\times[0,h]\) against the wall \(x\le0\), take \(p=(q,0,0)\), \(v=(0,q,0)\) and \(\omega=(0,0,1)\), with \(q\ge0\). For \(0<t<\pi/2\), \(-a<q\tan(t/2)<b\) and \(0<b\tan t-q(\sec t-1)<w\), the overlap is an uncapped triangle and

\[ V(t)=\frac{h[b\sin t-q(1-\cos t)]^2}{2\sin t\cos t} =h\left(\frac{b^2}2t-\frac{bq}2t^2+ \left(\frac{b^2}6+\frac{q^2}8\right)t^3\right)+O(t^4). \]

All these paths have the same initial velocity field. When \(q=0\), the quadratic term vanishes and the exact branch is \(h b^2\tan(t)/2\). At \(t_*=\arctan(w/b)\), the far side becomes active and the next branch is \(h[wb-w^2\cot(t)/2]\). Value and first derivative agree at this event, while second derivatives do not. Extrapolating the old branch through the event is invalid. These bounded prism formulas do not extend the translation API to generic rotating polyhedra.

docs.title: Current BRepAX Implementation
docs.text:
Method C in brepax.boolean.stratum uses a custom VJP:

  1. The forward value samples a hard Boolean indicator on a finite grid. Exact min/max set composition does not make quadrature exact.
  2. Sampled SDF signs select a relation label. Small overlap or protrusion regions can be missed. There is no explicit exact-contact classification.
  3. Disjoint and contained cases use primitive-volume derivatives when finite analytical formulas exist. Exactness requires both correct classification and correct formulas; unbounded primitives use a grid estimate instead.
  4. Partial overlap differentiates a sigmoid indicator on the frozen grid, with width equal to the geometric mean cell spacing.

The backward rule is a surrogate for a continuous geometric derivative, generally not the derivative of the hard sampled forward value. Three simple labels with analytical formulas do not imply accuracy on three quarters of configurations or solve moving intersection boundaries.

The analytical disk reference also uses distance floors and angle clipping. Near contact, independent limits or stable formulas must distinguish these safeguards from the mathematical derivative. See the safe-primal discussion.

docs.title: Invariance and Numerical Evidence
docs.text:
Exact area/volume is invariant under common rigid motion. Uniform length scaling by \(s>0\) scales \(n\)-dimensional measure by \(s^n\) and gradients with respect to lengths by \(s^{n-1}\); center gradients rotate with geometry. Grid orientation, finite windows, smoothing widths, and sampled detection can break or approximate these laws. Dimensional tolerances and smoothing parameters must scale with units.

Separate value error, relation detection, derivative error, and optimization outcome. At nonsmooth events compare one-sided limits; away from events, sweep finite-difference steps and resolution against an independent oracle. Relative error alone is misleading when the true derivative tends to zero.

Selected-fixture errors are not universal convergence rates or gradient-sign guarantees. AD through a frozen mesh likewise does not establish derivatives of regenerated CAD with moving trims or changing topology. See the design thesis and TOI discussion.

docs.title: Event-Time Sensitivity and the Limits of TOI Correction
docs.text: Method B is unimplemented. The valid calculation below differentiates an event time; it does not derive an exact correction to a static Boolean volume gradient. Earlier versions conflated these objects and gave incompatible signs for the proposed gradient and VJP.

docs.title: Boundary Functions
docs.text:
For disks with positive radii and center distance \(d=\|c_1-c_2\|\):

\[ g_{\mathrm{ext}}(\theta)=d-r_1-r_2,\qquad g_{\mathrm{int}}(\theta)=|r_1-r_2|-d. \]

Partial overlap satisfies both guards strictly negative. Equal radii and coincident centers can make the internal guard nonsmooth and need separate treatment. Ordinary disk area and sphere volume are \(C^1\) at both external and unequal-radius internal tangency; see Stratification Theory.

docs.title: Derivative of a Simple Event Time
docs.text:
Fix a direction \(v\) and path \( heta(t)= heta_0+t v\) in the valid parameter domain. Suppose a smooth guard \(g\) has a finite isolated root \( au>0\), the selected root remains the same local event, and

\[ abla g( heta_ au)^ op v e0,\qquad heta_ au= heta_0+ au v. \]

The implicit function theorem applied to \(g( heta_0+ au v)=0\) gives

\[ D_{ heta_0} au =- rac{ abla g( heta_ au)^ op}{ abla g( heta_ au)^ op v}. \]

This differentiates the event time with respect to initial parameters, holding \(v\) fixed. If \(v\) depends on \( heta_0\), its derivative also enters. Selecting the first of multiple roots introduces event-order changes not covered by this local formula.

A zero denominator means transversality fails, not that no event exists. For example, \(g(t)=\sqrt{4+(t-1)^2}-2\) has finite contact at \(t=1\) with \(g'(1)=0\). Clamping the denominator or returning zero defines a fallback, not a justified derivative.

docs.title: Why This Is Not a Static Gradient Correction
docs.text:
A future event on a chosen path does not alter the local derivative of \(f( heta_0)\). An exact volume locally independent of a center coordinate has zero derivative in that direction.

The earlier rule added \([( abla f_j- abla f_i)^ op v]D_{ heta_0} au\) to \( abla f_i\). Take \(f(x)=\max(0,x)\), \(x_0=-1\), \(v=1\), and guard \(g(x)=x\). Then \( au=1\), \(D_{x_0} au=-1\), and the derivative jump is \(1\). The proposed rule returns \(-1\) instead of the true static derivative \(0\). The former VJP used the opposite sign and returned \(+1\), also incorrect.

Event-time sensitivity can enter a specified look-ahead objective or a trajectory/update-map derivative. A deliberately nonlocal optimization signal is another possibility. Each needs its own contract and validation; none follows from adding a future derivative jump to a static gradient.

docs.title: Contact Dynamics and JAX
docs.text:
Hybrid dynamics differentiates a flow with guards and reset maps. A saltation matrix describes sensitivity across a transition. Static Boolean volume has no such flow/reset map by default. Sharing an implicit-function calculation is an analogy, not a mathematical isomorphism. See Kong et al., Saltation Matrices.

A JVP must be linear in its tangent input, while its coefficients can depend nonlinearly on primal values. Residual dependence alone does not require jax.custom_vjp. See JAX custom derivative rules.

docs.title: Implementation Status
docs.text: brepax.boolean.toi has no implementation; method="toi" raises NotImplementedError. ADR-0009 retains the deferral. A future method must first specify whether it differentiates static geometry, an event time, or a trajectory, including grazing and simultaneous events.

docs.title: Why B-Rep
docs.text: Why BRepAX operates on true Boundary Representation geometry rather than implicit (SDF) representations alone.

docs.title: The Limitation of Implicit Representations
docs.text:
SDF-based and implicit shape representations are powerful for differentiable geometry, but they cannot capture:

  • Parametric surfaces: NURBS, Bezier patches, and analytic surfaces (planes, cylinders, cones, tori) with exact evaluation
  • Trim curves: The boundaries that define which portion of a surface is active in a face
  • Tolerance handling: Manufacturing tolerances that determine whether edges are coincident or distinct
  • Face/edge/vertex incidence: The combinatorial structure that encodes how geometric entities connect

These are precisely the structures that manufacturing cost analysis depends on (undercuts, wall thickness, rib detection, mold direction, bend analysis).

docs.title: Existing Work in the Implicit Space
docs.text:
Several projects already address differentiable implicit geometry:

  • Marschner et al.'s pseudo-SDF correction
  • DreamCAD and related neural implicit CAD methods
  • MeshSDF and DMTet for differentiable mesh extraction

BRepAX's differentiation from these approaches comes from operating directly on B-Rep topology, not from JAX-nativeness alone.

docs.title: OCCT as the Foundation
docs.text:
Open CASCADE Technology (OCCT) is the industry-standard open-source B-Rep kernel, used by FreeCAD, CadQuery, build123d, and many commercial systems. By building on OCCT, BRepAX gains:

  • Exact parametric surface evaluation (no tessellation artifacts)
  • Standard STEP file I/O for interoperability with industrial CAD systems
  • Robust Boolean operations as a reference implementation
  • Access to the full vocabulary of B-Rep topology

docs.title: STEP preparation and JAX evaluation
docs.text:
STEP reading and OCCT extraction run on the host, outside jit, vmap, and differentiation. The numerical kernels operate on the resulting arrays and geometric models; JAX transformation support follows each API's contract.

Face conversion and mesh extraction support planes, cylinders, spheres, cones, tori, and B-spline surfaces (including rational weights). Other OCCT surface types are unsupported. face_to_primitive warns and returns None for them; mesh extraction raises NotImplementedError rather than returning an incomplete mesh. CSG reconstruction also rejects unsupported faces. Successful conversion alone does not establish an accurate solid SDF.

extract_mesh_topology and evaluate_mesh separate OCCT preparation from JAX vertex evaluation. Connectivity and the extracted UV samples form a fixed discretization; uv_scale_param can scale plane UV coordinates so that caps follow a linked parameter. Parameter changes must preserve closure and shared boundaries; a derivative of this discretization is not a derivative through OCCT reconstruction or remeshing. Topology-changing edits require separate validation.

docs.title: Mesh mass properties
docs.text:
For a watertight, consistently oriented mesh, the divergence theorem gives the mesh's signed volume. Accuracy against the original curved CAD depends on tessellation. The integration report records fixture measurements, not an error bound for every supported surface or input.

triangulate_shape evaluates each triangle corner from its own face's parameters independently, so a vertex on an edge shared by two faces gets two numerically close but generally distinct copies; the mesh is not literally watertight at the index level. triangulate_shape_watertight is an opt-in mode that instead welds shared vertices identified from OCCT's own per-edge mesh discretization (not a distance tolerance) and returns a WatertightMesh (vertices, faces, max_gap) whose vertices[faces] is a true index-level watertight mesh. WatertightMesh is a registered JAX pytree (an equinox.Module of arrays only), so jit and vmap can return it directly; host metadata such as surface_type and per-face triangle counts is not array data and lives instead on WatertightTopology, from extract_watertight_topology. A shared vertex's position is a two-level mean -- each incident face's own nodes there, then those per-face means across the vertex's distinct incident faces -- so jax.grad distributes symmetrically per incident face even when one face (e.g. at a periodic face's own seam) contributes more than one of its own nodes to that vertex. extract_watertight_topology and evaluate_watertight_mesh split the host-side OCCT extraction and validation from this averaging, a pure JAX function of explicit per-face parameters (B-spline degrees excluded -- they are shape-determining dispatch keys, not differentiable data, and stay on WatertightTopology so a traced call never needs to hash one), so a caller can differentiate, jit, or vmap with respect to specific per-face surface parameters without repeating the OCCT work. WatertightMesh.max_gap reports an upper bound on the largest disagreement between any two of a shared vertex's incident nodes -- computed from their raw evaluations, not the per-face means used for vertices, so it still catches two nodes of the same face disagreeing (e.g. across a periodic face's own seam) -- and an optional tolerance argument rejects a mesh whose evaluations disagree by more than that bound instead of silently welding through the disagreement.

Function Numerical contract divergence_volume Cubic polynomial in triangle vertices; signed volume in length cubed. mesh_surface_area Sum of triangle areas, in length squared; uses a norm, not a polynomial. Collapsed triangles use a chosen zero subgradient. mesh_center_of_mass First moments divided by volume, in length units; undefined for nonempty zero-volume inputs. mesh_inertia_tensor Tensor about the center of mass at unit density, in length to the fifth power; requires nonzero volume and outward orientation.

Nearly degenerate solids can make the normalized moments ill-conditioned. See the function contracts below for empty-input behavior and other assumptions.

docs.title: Boolean measures and trimmed surfaces
docs.text:
Union, intersection, and subtraction have stratum-dispatched measure implementations. Where finite primitive volume formulas apply, disjoint and contained configurations use analytical gradients. Intersecting configurations and other fallbacks differentiate a smoothed indicator on a frozen grid as a surrogate for the hard sampled forward measure. These estimators have discretization error and do not establish exact derivatives through arbitrary CAD topology changes. See Boolean operations for the APIs.

Standalone trimmed-face distances and CSG half-space composition have different contracts. TrimmedCSGStump uses raw primitive SDFs in its DNF composition, including B-splines; trim frames are retained as metadata. ADR-0020 explains why the trim-aware blend is excluded from that composition. See NURBS differentiation scope for the remaining distinction between surface, face, and solid derivatives.

docs.title: brepax.io.step.read_step(path)
docs.text:
Read a STEP file and return the top-level shape.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default path str | Path

Path to the STEP file (.step or .stp).

required

Returns:

Type Description TopoDS_Shape

The parsed OCCT shape.

Raises:

Type Description FileNotFoundError

If the file does not exist.

ValueError

If the STEP file cannot be parsed.

Source code in src/brepax/io/step.py 
def read_step(path: str | Path) -> TopoDS_Shape:
    """Read a STEP file and return the top-level shape.

    Args:
        path: Path to the STEP file (.step or .stp).

    Returns:
        The parsed OCCT shape.

    Raises:
        FileNotFoundError: If the file does not exist.
        ValueError: If the STEP file cannot be parsed.
    """
    resolved = Path(path).resolve()
    if not resolved.is_file():
        msg = f"STEP file not found: {resolved}"
        raise FileNotFoundError(msg)

    reader = STEPControl_Reader()
    status = reader.ReadFile(str(resolved))
    if status != IFSelect_RetDone:
        msg = f"Failed to read STEP file (status={status}): {resolved}"
        raise ValueError(msg)

    reader.TransferRoots()
    shape = reader.OneShape()
    if shape.IsNull():
        msg = f"STEP file produced a null shape: {resolved}"
        raise ValueError(msg)

    return shape

docs.title: brepax.brep.convert.face_to_primitive(face)
docs.text:
Convert a single OCP face to a BRepAX Primitive.

Maps planes, cylinders, spheres, cones, tori, and B-spline surfaces (including rational weights) to BRepAX primitives, extracting geometric parameters via OCCT adaptor classes. This is host-side preparation.

Returns None with a warning for other surface types.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default face TopoDS_Face

An OCCT topological face.

required

Returns:

Name Type Description A Primitive | None

class:Primitive instance, or None if the surface type

Primitive | None

is not supported.

Source code in src/brepax/brep/convert.py 
def face_to_primitive(face: TopoDS_Face) -> Primitive | None:
    """Convert a single OCP face to a BRepAX Primitive.

    Maps planes, cylinders, spheres, cones, tori, and B-spline surfaces
    (including rational weights) to BRepAX primitives, extracting geometric
    parameters via OCCT adaptor classes. This is host-side preparation.

    Returns None with a warning for other surface types.

    Args:
        face: An OCCT topological face.

    Returns:
        A :class:`Primitive` instance, or ``None`` if the surface type
        is not supported.
    """
    adaptor = BRepAdaptor_Surface(face)
    stype = adaptor.GetType()

    if stype == GeomAbs_Plane:
        gp_plane = adaptor.Plane()
        point = _gp_pnt_to_array(gp_plane.Location())
        normal = _gp_dir_to_array(gp_plane.Axis().Direction())
        offset = jnp.dot(normal, point)
        return PlanePrim(normal=normal, offset=offset)

    if stype == GeomAbs_Cylinder:
        gp_cyl = adaptor.Cylinder()
        point = _gp_pnt_to_array(gp_cyl.Location())
        axis = _gp_dir_to_array(gp_cyl.Axis().Direction())
        radius = jnp.array(gp_cyl.Radius())
        return CylinderPrim(point=point, axis=axis, radius=radius)

    if stype == GeomAbs_Sphere:
        gp_sph = adaptor.Sphere()
        center = _gp_pnt_to_array(gp_sph.Location())
        radius = jnp.array(gp_sph.Radius())
        return SpherePrim(center=center, radius=radius)

    if stype == GeomAbs_Cone:
        gp_cone = adaptor.Cone()
        apex = _gp_pnt_to_array(gp_cone.Apex())
        axis = _gp_dir_to_array(gp_cone.Axis().Direction())
        angle = jnp.array(abs(gp_cone.SemiAngle()))
        return ConePrim(apex=apex, axis=axis, angle=angle)

    if stype == GeomAbs_Torus:
        gp_torus = adaptor.Torus()
        center = _gp_pnt_to_array(gp_torus.Location())
        axis = _gp_dir_to_array(gp_torus.Axis().Direction())
        major_radius = jnp.array(gp_torus.MajorRadius())
        minor_radius = jnp.array(gp_torus.MinorRadius())
        return TorusPrim(
            center=center,
            axis=axis,
            major_radius=major_radius,
            minor_radius=minor_radius,
        )

    if stype == GeomAbs_BSplineSurface:
        return _convert_bspline_face(adaptor, face)

    type_name = _SURFACE_TYPE_NAMES.get(stype, "unknown")
    warnings.warn(
        f"Unsupported surface type: {type_name}, skipping face",
        stacklevel=2,
    )
    return None

docs.title: brepax.brep.triangulate
docs.text:
Triangulation of B-Rep faces for divergence theorem volume.

Uses OCCT BRepMesh for watertight mesh topology, then re-evaluates vertex positions inside the JAX computation graph using parametric surface functions. This gives jax.grad flow from volume through triangle vertices to primitive parameters (control points, radius, etc.) while preserving mesh watertightness.

triangulate_shape evaluates each triangle corner from its own face's parameters independently, so a vertex on a shared edge gets two numerically close but distinct copies: watertight as a surface covering, but not at the index level. triangulate_shape_watertight additionally welds those copies into one vertex per physical point, identified from OCCT edge topology rather than a distance tolerance; extract_watertight_topology and evaluate_watertight_mesh split that into frozen host-side topology and a pure JAX re-evaluation function, for differentiating with respect to specific per-face surface parameters without repeating the OCCT work. See their docstrings and ADR-0024 for the design rationale.

docs.title: WatertightMesh
docs.text:
Bases: Module

Welded, consistently oriented mesh from :func:evaluate_watertight_mesh.

A registered JAX pytree (an :class:equinox.Module) of arrays only, so it can be returned from -- not just passed through -- jax.jit and jax.vmap. Host metadata (surface_type, per-face triangle counts) lives on :class:WatertightTopology instead, since it is not itself array data; correlate it with faces via WatertightTopology.n_triangles_per_face.

vertices[faces] reproduces the (n, 3, 3) triangle-corner layout :func:triangulate_shape returns, so it can be passed directly to :func:divergence_volume, :func:mesh_surface_area, and the other mesh metrics in this module.

docs.title: faces instance-attribute
docs.text: Triangle connectivity into vertices.

docs.title: max_gap instance-attribute
docs.text: An upper bound on the largest disagreement between any two of a shared vertex's incident nodes (not the per-face means used for vertices): twice the largest distance from any individual node's own independent evaluation to that vertex's final welded position. By the triangle inequality this bounds the true largest pairwise gap between any two incident nodes' evaluations, including a disagreement between two nodes on the same face (e.g. both sides of a periodic face's own seam), which the face-weighted mean used for vertices does not by itself expose. A large value indicates surface reconstructions that disagree at a shared boundary; see the tolerance argument of :func:triangulate_shape_watertight.

docs.title: vertices instance-attribute
docs.text: Welded vertex positions. Each row is the mean, over every incident face, of that face's own mean of its (one or more) nodes at this vertex -- see :func:evaluate_watertight_mesh -- so jax.grad distributes symmetrically across incident faces, weighted by face, not by node.

docs.title: WatertightTopology dataclass
docs.text:
Frozen host-side topology feeding :func:evaluate_watertight_mesh.

Produced once per shape by :func:extract_watertight_topology (OCCT meshing, edge-topology welding, and manifold validation -- all outside jit/vmap/differentiation), then reused for repeated differentiable re-evaluation with different per-face surface parameters, analogous to :func:extract_mesh_topology and :func:evaluate_mesh for the non-welded mesh. Not itself a registered pytree: it is meant to be closed over or passed as a static argument, never returned from or traced by jit/vmap.

docs.title: face_records instance-attribute
docs.text: Per-face host data: surface_type, us, vs, n_points, and -- for a "bspline" face -- the B-spline degrees deg_u, deg_v. Degrees are shape-determining metadata (they select which batched evaluator to dispatch to and are used as dict/cache keys), so they live here, not in params_list, and stay concrete Python ints even when evaluate_watertight_mesh is called under jax.jit.

docs.title: faces instance-attribute
docs.text: Triangle connectivity into the welded vertices, (n_triangles, 3), int32; already filtered to drop zero-area triangles (a full-revolution pole or apex can leave OCCT's own mesh with one spanning two now-welded copies of that point, which contributed exactly zero area and volume before welding).

docs.title: n_triangles_per_face instance-attribute
docs.text: Post-filtering triangle count for each face, in face_records order. Can differ from :func:triangulate_shape's count for the same face because of the zero-area triangles faces drops.

docs.title: node_vertex instance-attribute
docs.text: Flattened (face, local node) index -> welded vertex index directly (pair_vertex[pair_of]), used for the raw per-node gap in WatertightMesh.max_gap.

docs.title: pair_of instance-attribute
docs.text: Flattened (face, local node) index -> (welded vertex, face) pair index.

docs.title: pair_vertex instance-attribute
docs.text: (welded vertex, face) pair index -> welded vertex index.

docs.title: params_list instance-attribute
docs.text: Default per-face surface parameters extracted from OCCT, in face_records order, with B-spline degrees excluded (see face_records). Pass to :func:evaluate_watertight_mesh, or a modified copy of it to differentiate with respect to specific per-face parameters.

docs.title: triangulate_shape(shape, *, deflection=_DEFAULT_DEFLECTION)
docs.text:
Triangulate all faces of a shape with JAX-native vertices.

Uses OCCT BRepMesh for watertight mesh topology, then re-evaluates each vertex position using JAX-native parametric surface functions. Faces are grouped by surface type (and BSpline signature) so each group is evaluated with a single batched jax.vmap, eliminating per-face Python dispatch overhead.

Each triangle corner is evaluated independently from its own face's parameters: a vertex shared by two faces gets two numerically close but generally distinct copies (see :func:triangulate_shape_watertight for a mode that welds them to a single, shared vertex). This is the original, unchanged contract depended on by existing callers.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default shape TopoDS_Shape

An OCCT topological shape.

required deflection float

Mesh deflection tolerance for OCCT tessellation.

_DEFAULT_DEFLECTION

Returns:

Type Description ndarray

Tuple of (triangles, params_list) where triangles has

list[dict[str, Any]]

shape (n_total, 3, 3) and params_list contains one

tuple[ndarray, list[dict[str, Any]]]

parameter dict per face, in traversal order.

Raises:

Type Description NotImplementedError

An evaluated face has an unsupported surface type.

ValueError

An evaluated face has no triangulation or no triangles.

If solids are present, only their faces are evaluated. Otherwise all faces are evaluated. A shape with no faces returns empty arrays and metadata.

docs.title: triangulate_shape_watertight(shape, *, deflection=_DEFAULT_DEFLECTION, tolerance=None)
docs.text:
Triangulate a shape into a single welded, watertight mesh.

Unlike :func:triangulate_shape, which gives each triangle corner an independent evaluation from its own face (so a shared edge gets two numerically close but distinct copies), this welds shared vertices identified from OCCT's own per-edge mesh discretization (topology and the edge's own curve parameter, not a vertex distance tolerance) and averages every incident face's own evaluation there, producing one vertex per physical point with gradients that flow symmetrically to every incident face's parameters. Degenerate edges (poles, apices) and a periodic face's seam are handled explicitly (see :func:_weld_shared_vertices).

A convenience composition of :func:extract_watertight_topology (host extraction and validation) and :func:evaluate_watertight_mesh (differentiable re-evaluation). Call those directly to re-evaluate the same topology under jax.jit, jax.vmap, or jax.grad against specific per-face parameters without repeating the OCCT work.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default shape TopoDS_Shape

An OCCT topological shape.

required deflection float

Mesh deflection tolerance for OCCT tessellation.

_DEFAULT_DEFLECTION tolerance float | None

If given, raise when WatertightMesh.max_gap (an upper bound on the largest gap between any two nodes' independent evaluations at a shared vertex) exceeds it. Pass the shape's own CAD tolerance (e.g. :func:brepax.experimental.applications. _hole_geometry.shape_tolerance) to reject faces whose reconstructions disagree by more than the model already tolerates. None (default) never raises on the gap; the value is still returned in max_gap for the caller to inspect.

None

Returns:

Name Type Description A WatertightMesh

class:WatertightMesh.

Raises:

Type Description NotImplementedError

An evaluated face has an unsupported surface type.

ValueError

A face has no triangulation; a shared edge cannot be identified from OCCT topology (see :func:_weld_shared_vertices); the welded result is not a closed, manifold, consistently oriented mesh; or tolerance is given and exceeded.

Examples:

>>> shape = read_step("model.step")
>>> mesh = triangulate_shape_watertight(shape, tolerance=1e-4)
>>> vol = divergence_volume(mesh.vertices[mesh.faces])
>>> grad = jax.grad(
...     lambda v: divergence_volume(v[mesh.faces])
... )(mesh.vertices)

docs.title: extract_watertight_topology(shape, *, deflection=_DEFAULT_DEFLECTION)
docs.text:
Host-side extraction and validation for a welded watertight mesh.

Meshes shape, identifies shared vertices from OCCT edge topology (see :func:_weld_shared_vertices), and validates that the welded result is a closed, manifold, consistently oriented mesh whose every vertex's incident triangles form a single fan (see :func:_check_manifold_closed and :func:_check_vertex_links_manifold). All of this runs once, on the host, outside any JAX transformation; :func:evaluate_watertight_mesh does the repeated, differentiable part.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default shape TopoDS_Shape

An OCCT topological shape.

required deflection float

Mesh deflection tolerance for OCCT tessellation.

_DEFAULT_DEFLECTION

Returns:

Name Type Description A WatertightTopology

class:WatertightTopology.

Raises:

Type Description NotImplementedError

An evaluated face has an unsupported surface type.

ValueError

A face has no triangulation, or the welded result is not a closed, manifold, consistently oriented mesh.

Examples:

>>> topology = extract_watertight_topology(shape)
>>> mesh = evaluate_watertight_mesh(topology, topology.params_list)
>>> vol = divergence_volume(mesh.vertices[mesh.faces])

docs.title: evaluate_watertight_mesh(topology, params_list)
docs.text:
Re-evaluate a welded mesh's vertices from explicit per-face parameters.

For each face, evaluates its own surface function at its stored UV coordinates using params_list (JAX-native, so jax.grad flows from the result through these parameters). A shared vertex's position is a two-level mean: first the mean of each incident face's own node evaluations at that vertex (collapsing, for example, both sides of a periodic face's own seam to one value per face), then the mean of those per-face means across the vertex's distinct incident faces. The second level is what keeps the result -- and its gradient -- weighted equally per incident face regardless of how many of that face's own nodes happen to coincide there. WatertightMesh.max_gap is computed separately, directly from the raw per-node evaluations (before either level of averaging), so it still exposes a disagreement the position averaging would otherwise hide, including between two nodes of the same face.

params_list entries hold only differentiable arrays (for a B-spline face, no deg_u/deg_v: see WatertightTopology. face_records), so this is a pure function of params_list with topology held static, and it supports jax.jit, jax.vmap, and differentiation the same way :func:evaluate_mesh does for the non-welded mesh -- including returning its WatertightMesh result directly from a jitted or vmapped function.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default topology WatertightTopology

Frozen topology from :func:extract_watertight_topology.

required params_list list[dict[str, Any]]

One parameter dict per face, in topology.face_records order; typically topology.params_list or a modified copy of it (e.g. with one face's control points perturbed).

required

Returns:

Name Type Description A WatertightMesh

class:WatertightMesh.

Examples:

>>> topology = extract_watertight_topology(shape)
>>> def volume_of(radius, face_index):
...     params = [dict(p) for p in topology.params_list]
...     params[face_index] = {**params[face_index], "radius": radius}
...     mesh = evaluate_watertight_mesh(topology, params)
...     return divergence_volume(mesh.vertices[mesh.faces])
>>> grad = jax.grad(volume_of)(jnp.array(5.0), 0)

docs.title: extract_mesh_topology(shape, *, deflection=_DEFAULT_DEFLECTION)
docs.text:
Extract watertight mesh topology from an OCCT shape.

Tessellates the shape via OCCT BRepMesh, then extracts per-face UV coordinates, triangle connectivity, and surface parameters. The returned data is static (not in the JAX graph) and serves as input to :func:evaluate_mesh for differentiable vertex re-evaluation.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default shape TopoDS_Shape

An OCCT topological shape.

required deflection float

Mesh deflection tolerance for OCCT tessellation.

_DEFAULT_DEFLECTION

Returns:

Type Description list[dict[str, Any]]

List of face dicts, each containing us, vs (numpy),

list[dict[str, Any]]

conn (numpy int32), reverse (bool), and surface

list[dict[str, Any]]

parameters (JAX arrays).

Raises:

Type Description NotImplementedError

An evaluated face has an unsupported surface type.

ValueError

An evaluated face has no triangulation or no triangles.

Face selection and empty-shape behavior follow :func:triangulate_shape.

Examples:

>>> topology = extract_mesh_topology(shape)
>>> triangles = evaluate_mesh(topology)
>>> vol = divergence_volume(triangles)

docs.title: evaluate_mesh(topology, overrides=None, *, uv_scale_param=None)
docs.text:
Re-evaluate mesh vertices from topology with parameter overrides.

For each face, evaluates the surface function at the stored UV coordinates using surface parameters. Any parameter in overrides replaces the corresponding stored value, allowing jax.grad to flow from volume through vertices to the overridden design parameter.

When uv_scale_param is set, plane faces scale their UV coordinates by overrides[uv_scale_param] / uv_scale_ref so that flat caps follow curved-surface parameter changes (e.g. disk caps scale with cylinder radius).

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default topology list[dict[str, Any]]

Face list from :func:extract_mesh_topology.

required overrides dict[str, ndarray] | None

Parameter name-value pairs to override.

None uv_scale_param str | None

Override key used to scale plane UV coordinates. Required for multi-face optimization where flat caps must track a curved-surface parameter.

None

Returns:

Type Description ndarray

Triangle vertices, shape (n_total, 3, 3).

Examples:

>>> topology = extract_mesh_topology(cylinder_shape)
>>> def volume_fn(radius):
...     return divergence_volume(
...         evaluate_mesh(topology, {"radius": radius},
...                       uv_scale_param="radius")
...     )
>>> grad = jax.grad(volume_fn)(jnp.array(5.0))

docs.title: divergence_volume(triangles)
docs.text:
Compute volume of a closed triangle mesh via the divergence theorem.

Uses the signed-tetrahedra formula in a local frame near the mesh: each triangle and the local origin form a tetrahedron whose signed volume is v0 . (v1 x v2) / 6. The sum over all triangles gives the enclosed volume for a watertight mesh with outward-facing normals.

Local coordinates reduce cancellation for solids far from the world origin. Units are length cubed. Empty meshes return zero.

jax.grad differentiates the frozen mesh. Geometric shape derivatives require shared boundaries to move consistently and preserve closure; independently moving duplicated triangle corners can open the mesh.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default triangles ndarray

Triangle vertices, shape (n, 3, 3).

required

Returns:

Type Description ndarray

Enclosed volume (scalar).

Examples:

>>> shape = read_step("model.step")
>>> tris, params = triangulate_shape(shape)
>>> vol = divergence_volume(tris)
>>> grad = jax.grad(divergence_volume)(tris)

docs.title: mesh_surface_area(triangles)
docs.text:
Compute surface area of a triangle mesh.

Sums the area of each triangle: (1/2) ||cross(e1, e2)||. Units are length squared. No absolute area floor is applied. Collapsed or collinear triangles have zero area with a chosen zero subgradient at the nondifferentiable point. Empty meshes return zero.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default triangles ndarray

Triangle vertices, shape (n, 3, 3).

required

Returns:

Type Description ndarray

Total surface area (scalar).

Examples:

>>> tris, _ = triangulate_shape(shape)
>>> area = mesh_surface_area(tris)

docs.title: mesh_center_of_mass(triangles)
docs.text:
Compute center of mass of a closed triangle mesh.

Integrates signed tetrahedron first moments in a local frame, then divides by signed volume. This avoids cancelling world-origin moments and introducing a dimensionful epsilon into the denominator.

Assumes a watertight mesh with nonzero volume. Units are length. Empty meshes return zero. For nonempty zero-volume inputs the center is undefined; nearly degenerate solids are ill-conditioned. Shape derivatives require closure-preserving shared-boundary motion.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default triangles ndarray

Triangle vertices, shape (n, 3, 3).

required

Returns:

Type Description ndarray

Center of mass, shape (3,).

Examples:

>>> tris, _ = triangulate_shape(shape)
>>> com = mesh_center_of_mass(tris)

docs.title: mesh_inertia_tensor(triangles)
docs.text:
Compute the inertia tensor of a closed triangle mesh about its center of mass.

Integrates signed tetrahedron moments (Tonon 2005), then applies the parallel axis theorem in a local frame near the center of mass. See https://doi.org/10.3844/jmssp.2005.8.11 for tetrahedron moments.

Assumes a watertight, outward-oriented mesh with nonzero volume and uniform density rho = 1. Empty meshes return zero. Length units L give inertia units L**5; uniform scaling by s multiplies the tensor by s**5. Nearly degenerate solids are ill-conditioned.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default triangles ndarray

Triangle vertices, shape (n, 3, 3).

required

Returns:

Type Description ndarray

Symmetric 3x3 inertia tensor about center of mass.

Examples:

>>> tris, _ = triangulate_shape(shape)
>>> I = mesh_inertia_tensor(tris)

docs.title: disk_disk
docs.text:
Closed-form solutions for two-disk Boolean operations.

Provides analytically differentiable union area, stratum classification, and boundary distance for pairs of 2D disks. Used as ground truth for validating numerical gradient methods.

docs.title: disk_disk_boundary_distance(c1, r1, c2, r2)
docs.text:
Distance from current configuration to the nearest stratum boundary.

Measures the minimum of distance to external tangency (d = r1 + r2) and internal tangency (d = |r1 - r2|).

Source code in src/brepax/analytical/disk_disk.py 
def disk_disk_boundary_distance(
    c1: Float[Array, "2"],
    r1: Float[Array, ""],
    c2: Float[Array, "2"],
    r2: Float[Array, ""],
) -> Float[Array, ""]:
    """Distance from current configuration to the nearest stratum boundary.

    Measures the minimum of distance to external tangency (d = r1 + r2)
    and internal tangency (d = |r1 - r2|).
    """
    d = jnp.linalg.norm(c1 - c2)
    dist_external = jnp.abs(d - (r1 + r2))
    dist_internal = jnp.abs(d - jnp.abs(r1 - r2))
    return jnp.minimum(dist_external, dist_internal)

docs.title: disk_disk_stratum_label(c1, r1, c2, r2)
docs.text:
Classify the topological stratum of a two-disk configuration.

Returns:

Type Description Integer[Array, '']

Integer-valued scalar: 0 = disjoint, 1 = intersecting, 2 = contained.

Source code in src/brepax/analytical/disk_disk.py 
def disk_disk_stratum_label(
    c1: Float[Array, "2"],
    r1: Float[Array, ""],
    c2: Float[Array, "2"],
    r2: Float[Array, ""],
) -> Integer[Array, ""]:
    """Classify the topological stratum of a two-disk configuration.

    Returns:
        Integer-valued scalar: 0 = disjoint, 1 = intersecting, 2 = contained.
    """
    d = jnp.linalg.norm(c1 - c2)
    return jnp.where(
        d >= r1 + r2,
        0,
        jnp.where(d <= jnp.abs(r1 - r2), 2, 1),
    )

docs.text:
Compute the union area of two disks analytically.

Uses the standard two-circle intersection area formula: A_union = A_1 + A_2 - A_intersection.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default c1 Float[Array, 2]

Center of disk 1.

required r1 Float[Array, '']

Radius of disk 1.

required c2 Float[Array, 2]

Center of disk 2.

Radius of disk 2.

required

Returns:

Type Description Float[Array, '']

Union area as a scalar.

Source code in src/brepax/analytical/disk_disk.py 
def disk_disk_union_area(
    c1: Float[Array, "2"],
    r1: Float[Array, ""],
    c2: Float[Array, "2"],
    r2: Float[Array, ""],
) -> Float[Array, ""]:
    """Compute the union area of two disks analytically.

    Uses the standard two-circle intersection area formula:
    A_union = A_1 + A_2 - A_intersection.

    Args:
        c1: Center of disk 1.
        r1: Radius of disk 1.
        c2: Center of disk 2.
        r2: Radius of disk 2.

    Returns:
        Union area as a scalar.
    """
    d = jnp.linalg.norm(c1 - c2)
    area1 = jnp.pi * r1**2
    area2 = jnp.pi * r2**2
    intersection = _intersection_area(d, r1, r2)
    return area1 + area2 - intersection

Uses the spherical cap intersection formula: V_union = V_1 + V_2 - V_intersection.
